Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m.
Prayers.
Prime Minister—Electricity Market and Skycity Convention Centre Legislation
1. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by all his statements?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Why does he stand by his statement on the prices New Zealanders
are paying for power: “I think that they are paying a price … in relation to the
environment we find ourselves in,”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Because it is true.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Did he fulfil his undertaking to the House yesterday to check the
figures that show New Zealand households will pay an extra $370 on average for power
because his Government insists on taking out $1.16 billion in Transpower dividends?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, but I did two things yesterday. One was that I went and
looked on the Infratil website to see how it is bagging the Labour Party for misleading
the country—

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: I raise a point of orde r, Mr Speaker. That pi ece of information has
nothing to do with the question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think that on this occasion the Prime Minister has adequately
answered the question.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he accept that pulling divide nds out of a company that needs
to invest $5 billion to strengthen the network means that family power bills are hit
twice: first, to pay for the upgrade, and then, second, to pay for his Government’s
dividend; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Dividends actually make no difference in terms of the pricing
of power. I am surprised the member does not know that. What actually sets the
transmission part of pricing is the Comm erce Commission’s weight ed average cost of
capital charging. It has got nothing to do with dividends. Secondly, yes, Transpower has
gone through a substantial upgrade. By the way, it started under Labour in 2005 when it
invested $252 million, and then in 2006 when it invested $288 million. So, yes, it has
invested about $3 billion, for which it will get its weighted average cost of capital
return, and that obviously has some impact . I suspect that what the Leader of the
Opposition should do is that he should go and look at this State-owned enterprise and
then he should go and look at another Stat e-owned enterprise called New Zealand Post,
because it has got a letter waiting for him from the Labour Party caucus.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: That was a strain. Does he think it is fair that his Cabinet awarded
the chief executive officer of Mighty River Power a 34 percent increase on top of a
$500,000 retention bonus at the same time as forcing New Zealand families to pay more
than $370 extra in power?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Decisions on remuneration are made by the board of Mighty
River Power. So the board of directors at  Mighty River Power said to Doug Heffernan,
their chief executive: “Doug, we love you.” But we know that in the Labour Party no
one would go to—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! That is sufficient.
11844 Questions for Oral Answer 10 Jul 2013

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Is he saying, therefore, that his Cabinet did not tick off the approval
for the chief executive officer to be aw arded a 34 percent pay increase and a $500,000
retention bonus; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: What I am saying is that decisions of compensation are made
by the board. Those decisions are held by the board. They may well tell the
Government, under a no-surprises policy, but they are made the board.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: How about answering the question?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Were you on the letter or not? Actually, last night—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! There is no need to bring the Speaker
into this debate.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Is he aware that under the Labour Government it did not take
dividends from Transpower, and instead invest ed it back into the company rather than
having to take dividends out and then ask consumers to pay for that?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Maybe I can answer that question by asking a question.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: No!

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I can see why your caucus meeting went so badly yesterday.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Could the Prime Minister ju st address the question that has
been asked.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: OK, I will address the questi on. Was Labour the Government
in 2002? If it was, it took a dividend from Transpower. Was it the Government in 2003?
If it was, it took a dividend from Transpower. Was it the Government in 2004? If it was,
it took a dividend from Transpower. Was it the Government—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! I have a point of order from the Hon
Annette King.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I believe that in question time  the members of the Opposition
ask the questions and the Mini sters answer. What we have had from the Prime Minister
is a series of questions back to the Labour Party.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] No, I need no assistance from the Prime
Minister. The question was asked and the Prime Minister chose his way of answering it.
It was addressed.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: How does the Prime Minister justify paying $1.9 million to
the “feed the schools” programmes and then $1.7 million to the chief executive officer
of Mighty River Power—how can that possibly be equitable or fair?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The two are not correlated. Fo r a start off, the Government
spends about $70 billion - odd a year, so you can go and draw any particular thing. But
in the end the compensation for the chie f executive of Might y River Power is
determined by the board. It might be that  he happened to be  doing a good job. I know
David Shearer is not, but Doug Heffernan—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Given the Prime Minister’s statement that he opposes a conscience
vote on the Skycity convention centre bill, what  pressure has he or his office placed on
National MPs to vote against their conscience on the first reading of the bill?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, I never said I opposed th at. What I said is that all
National MPs will be voting for the legislati on. The reason they will be voting for it is
that this party went on the campaign trail and campaigned on this issue. Every single
member of this party was elected on the back of that policy, just like the members of the
Green Party were elected on some of the mad policies that they campaigned on.
10 Jul 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 11845
Skycity, Convention Centre—Gambling-related Harm
2. HONE HARAWIRA (Leader—Mana)  to the Minister for Economic

items.speaker: Development
items.text: Does he think the Government’s  decision to grant 230 new pokie
machines, 52 new gambling tables, and a 35-year licence extension is worth the increase
in relationship breakdowns, depression, suic ide, family violence, increased money
laundering, job losses, increased problem gambling and financial problems, as identified
by its own Ministry of Business, Innovati on and Employment-compiled regulatory
impact statement; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I reject the
premise of the member’s question for a number of reasons. The first point is to note that
the regulatory impact statement states that  harm from gambling may include the things
the member refers to. It is also important that there are a number of things that mitigate
those possibilities in this case. Firstly, it is by no means clear at all that a marginal
increase in machines in one casino will in crease gambling harm, especially when the
total number of machines across Auckla nd and across New Zealand continues to
decline. Also, the negotiated significant a dditional harm-minimisation measures that
apply to all gambling machines across the casin o will together act to reduce harm. Once
the concessions are in place there is also absolutely nothing to stop the regulatory
authorities introducing new harm-minimisation measures over time.

items.speaker: Hone Harawira
items.text: When the Minister said yesterday that it is difficult to quantify the
potential size of any increased risk of ha rm, does that mean he did not read the full
regulatory impact statement from his own mi nistry, which said: “an additional 4,779 …
people may be at least partly affected by casino machines and an additional 3,600 … by
casino tables.”, and does he now  accept that the potential si ze of any increased risk of
harm is not only quantifiable but also unacceptable?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: No. In fact, the same statemen t—because it is important to
get this in context—says that it is difficult to quantify the potential risk of any increased
risk of harm. It goes on to say, in relation to the matters the member raises, that this is a
hypothesis, and says in paragraph 91: “it is possible to hypothesise”. It then goes on to
say: “It is difficult to estimate the additional numbers …” and “Putting a precise cost on
this potential increase is also difficult.” So it does r ecord a hypothesis as a possibility,
but, as I answered in answer to the primar y question, there are a number of things that
mitigate that.

items.speaker: Hone Harawira
items.text: Does the Minister accept that th e decision to grant 230 new pokie
machines, 52 new gambling tables, and a 35-yea r licence extension is evidence that this
Government operates on the basis that de liberately harming its own citizens is
acceptable, as long as it achieves its own prim ary goals of allowing its fat cat friends to
profiteer from New Zealanders ’ misery, and getting free ac cess for themselves; if not,
why not?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I reject that assertion completely. This Government is
focused on jobs and growth for New Zealanders . I appreciate that that member himself
is against jobs and growth for his constituen ts in Te Tai Tokerau. This Government is
focused on them. The reality is that many hu man activities have the potential for social
harm, but the important thing is how you mitigate that risk.
Tax System Changes—Impact on Families
3. MAGGIE BARRY (National—North Shore)  to the Minister of Finance : How
has the Government made the tax system  fairer for New Zealand households and
families?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Over successive Government
Budgets, the Government has made a number of  changes to make the system fairer. It
11846 Questions for Oral Answer 10 Jul 2013
has removed the ability set up by the Labour Government to enable people to shelter
their income in trusts, raised the effective tax rate on property investment, increased
funding for the Inland Revenue Department to target property speculators and others
avoiding tax, prevented people from using investment losses to make themselves
eligible for Working for Families and other Government support, and brought in stricter
rules to ensure multinational companies contri bute their fair share of tax. At the same
time, the Government has reduced income tax rates across the board. Almost three-
quarters of taxpayers now face a personal tax rate of 17.5 percent.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: What changes has the Government  made to income tax rates and
other taxes to help families get ahead?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: In 2010 our tax package redu ced tax on work and savings,
and increased taxes on consumption and prope rty speculation. After-tax incomes at all
levels of taxable income were immediately increased by more than the increase in GST
in 2010. The changes also made the tax system  fairer. Two-thirds of the cost of the
income tax cuts in 2010 went to reducing th e bottom two tax rates. So someone earning
$48,000 a year now has a top tax rate of 17.5 percent.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: How does the income tax system interact with income support
provided to lower-income families?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Despite a recession and signi ficant fiscal deficits, the
Government has maintained a redistribut ive tax and income support system that
supports low and middle income earners in Ne w Zealand. At any particular time a large
number of households, effectively, do not pay net tax. That is because the amount they
pay in income tax is exceeded by the am ount they receive from welfare benefits,
Working for Families, paid parental leave, accommodation subsidies, and others. This is
entirely appropriate to redistribute income  from the higher-income earners to those
genuinely in need.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: How significantly do the income tax and income support systems
redistribute incomes for New Zealand households?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: When we look at the way the system redistributes income,
we can measure that by net tax for income  groups—that is, the difference between the
tax they pay and the assistance that they receive. For families earning under $60,000 a
year, taking into account the income support payments and their income tax, they pay
$2.7 billion in income tax and receive $1.8 billion of income support. That is the total
for people earning under $60,000. The net effect of  that is that for households earning
over $150,000 it is 12 percent. The top 12 percent of income earners pay 76 percent of
net income tax.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Is the Minister aware that his superficial analysis of tax paid by
income group, firstly, takes no account of th e fact that low and middle income people
pay GST on the vast majority of their spen ding at higher effective tax rates than high-
income earners, and, secondly, ignores the advice of the OECD that in New Zealand
capital income earned by the wealthiest in society attracts virtually no taxation, which is
unfair; if he is not aware of  either of these things, does it not show that his latest
educational trip to the OECD was a waste of time and money?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, that is not true. If he is concerned about the capital gains
of the wealthy not being taxed, that is actually part of hi s policy, because he wants to
exempt the family home from his capital  gains tax. Secondly, when you look at the
distributional effects of GST, in fact, it is relatively neutral. The Labour Party has to get
used to the idea that the 2010 tax package reduc ed inequality in income tax distribution
in New Zealand.
10 Jul 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 11847
Skycity, Convention Centre—Harm Minimisation Plan and Consultation on
Legislative Changes
4. METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Minister for Economic

items.speaker: Development
items.text: When he said that gambling-related harm from the SkyCity deal would
be mitigated by “negotiated, significant addi tional harm minimisation measures” did he
mean measures additional to those the casino is already obliged to use; if so, how?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Yes. The
Government has negotiated a number of significant harm minimisation measures as part
of the agreement with Skycity. These in clude the introduction of the predictive
modelling tool, which analyses data to iden tify players at risk of problem gambling.
Skycity is also being required to implem ent a voluntary pre-commitment system, where
players can elect to restrict the amount of time they play or the amount they spend, and
this applies to all machines at all times in the casino and will become part of Skycity’s
host responsibility programme. It will also  have to introduce player identification
requirements when amounts over $500 are be ing put on to, or cashed from, ticket-in,
ticket-out machines in non-restricted area s, as well as, of course, doubling of the
number of host responsibil ity specialists to deliver 24-hours-a-day, 7-days-a-week
coverage in the casino.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: How many of the 13,000 people and 6,500 children whom his
advisers say will be harmed by this deal will not be harmed due to the supposedly
additional measures?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I reject again today the premise of the member’s question. I
have reviewed the regulatory impact statem ent fairly carefully, as you would expect,
and it makes it clear that actually being able to determine a level of additional harm is
not possible to do. They talk about a hypothesis, and it is very difficult to estimate the
additional numbers of people who may experi ence problems. They also say that putting
a precise cost on a potential increase is also difficult.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Will the Minister release all the advice he has received on the social
harms of the extra gambling in this deal  today so that when National MPs vote
tomorrow, they are fully informed about the extent of the social harms in his bill?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I will check again, but my  understanding is we have
released most of the information that we have. There is some more information in
regards to the negotiations, which will be rele ased in the next little while, but I think
particularly the key elements in relation to potential harm have b een released and are
also very adequately traversed in the regulatory impact statement.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Will the Minister explain to his colleagues before they vote
tomorrow why the New Zealand Police and the Ministry of Justice were excluded from
the discussions to introduce ticket-in, ti cket-out technology throughout the whole
casino, when his officials knew that those ministries would be concerned about the
increased risk of money-laundering?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am not sure that the member is correct on that, but
certainly it is fair to say that my colleague s in the caucus of the National Party have had
plenty of time, partly with assistance from  the member, to assess their level of support
for this particular arrangement, including, of  course, the ability to assess whether the
230 machines are an appropriate arrangement  to make for a very large convention
centre, compared with, say, 230 machines for one a quarter of  the size under the
previous Government supported by the Greens.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I seek leave to table an email received by me under the Official
Information Act dated 16 March 2012 from an  official who says: “As for Justice and
Police, they have obviously not been consulted on the details—”
11848 Questions for Oral Answer 10 Jul 2013

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There appears to be none. It can be tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Is it not the truth, Minister, th at the Minister is frightened of
supporting a genuine conscience vote on this bi ll because he knows that this bill, this
deal, is hanging by a one-vote thread?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am pretty confident, and I know that the Government is
pretty confident, about the votes on this si de of the House, but I appreciate there are
members on the other side of the House who might like the opportunity to vote for jobs
and growth through this bill. I note that the Labour leader , for example, has allowed a
conscience vote in this matter,  and given the state of the Labour caucus, I expect a few
more votes from them.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Is this Minister prepared to rule out using a process similar to
this for a convention centre in another city?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, I can tell the member that there are no plans at all that
I am aware of in this  respect. What he rais es is a hypothetical que stion, and we would
deal with it if it came up at the time, but there has been certainly nothing raised in that
regard.
Better Public Services Targets—Infant Immunisation and Rheumatic Fever
5. SHANE ARDERN (National— Taranaki - King Country)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Health
items.text: What is this Government doing, as part of Better Public Services, to ensure that
New Zealand children ar e better protected from preventa ble diseases such as whooping
cough and hepatitis B?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: New Zealand’s children are getting a
better start in life as a result of progre ss towards the Government’s Better Public
Services results, which include increasing in fant immunisation rate s so that 95 percent
of 8-month-olds are fully immunised by December 2014, and maintaining this through
to June 2017. The latest resu lts show 89 percent of 8-m onth-olds have been fully
immunised with their scheduled vaccinations , protecting them from serious diseases
such as whooping cough and hepatitis B, and we are on track to achieve the 95 percent
target.

items.speaker: Shane Ardern
items.text: What other work to protect pe ople from preventable diseases
contributes to the Government’s Better Public Services targets?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Very early indications from the Government’s programme to
reduce the incidence of rheumatic fever by tw o-thirds show a reduction in the incidence
rate for acute rheumatic fever initial hospitalisations, but this is only one set of data, and
so needs to be treated cauti ously. For the second Budget in a row this Government has
doubled its investment in the Rheumatic  Fever Prevention Programme, from $12
million, to $24 million, to $46 million in Budget 2013.
Solid Energy—Financial Position, Management, and Assistance
6. Hon DAVID PARKER (Labour)  to the Minister of Finance : Given his
statement yesterday that “Solid Energy wa s another example of where the incoming
National Government had to clean up a mess left by the previous Government”, what
was the level of debt held by Solid Energy on 30 June 2008 compared with the level of
debt on 30 June 2012, and what is the total amount of divi dends received by the Crown
from Solid Energy since he became Minister of Finance?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The amounts are $15 million, $295
million, and $163.9 million respectively.
10 Jul 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 11849

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Is the Minister of Finance aw are that the Labour Government
never approved of Solid Energy’s lignite developments, because of dubious economics
and greenhouse gas emissions, and that he, th e Minister, turned the first sod on Solid
Energy’s lignite plant; and how is that the previous Labour Government’s fault?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I think the member is mixing up a couple of pr ojects there.
One is the briquette plant, for which I did turn the first sod because it created jobs in a
community where 400 jobs had been lost. I know, of course, that the Opposition was
against the new jobs in Mataur a, even though a w hole lot of the people in Mataura vote
for the Labour Party. Now I am asking them why.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I seek leave to table a photograph of Mr English and a sod.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! No, I am not prepared to put that leave.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Is the Minister aware that hi s National Government encouraged
Solid Energy to expand its coal operati ons, take on more debt, and pay out higher
dividends, all in the face of a falling coal price; and how is that the fault of the previous
Labour Government?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I have to say that Solid Energy did not need any
encouragement. It had very large-scal e plans for expansion, which the current
Government disagreed with. Of course, we could have moved faster to slow down Solid
Energy’s investment, but when we did move , the Labour Party organised a protest on
the steps of Parliament, which means that we do not take its compla ints about this very
seriously.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I seek leave to table a document of Mr Brownlee’s—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am not prepared to ente rtain this any further. Would the
member continue with his supplementary questions, if he has any.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. Is it now out of order to
table photographs that are inconvenient to the Government?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is questioning a previous ruling.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Is it out of order for
members to seek leave to table photographs in this Parliament?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have given a substa ntial ruling on the tabling of
documents. If a document is of assistance to  members and gives them further, good
information, I will allow the leave to be put. In this case, the member is attempting to
play politics with a couple of photographs. I told him I would not put that leave. He
continued his point of order, which is an a buse of the privilege of a point of order and
will lead to disorder.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member has a right to ra ise a point of order, and it will
be heard in silence.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: My point of order is that we have had a Minister denying the
promotion of coal, and a member trying to  table a document that was promoted by a
current Minister of the House and described as “Sexy Coal”. It s eems inappropriate not
to allow a document entitled “Sexy Coal” to be tabled.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Again, that member is now dispu ting a ruling I have already given,
and I will take that very seriously if it happens again. Question No. 7.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Supplementary question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I had called Catherine Delahunty for Question No. 7.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Spea ker. What happened before was that
David Parker was raising a point of order w ith you when you indicated that you did not
want to hear it, so you moved on to the next question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That is exactly right.
11850 Questions for Oral Answer 10 Jul 2013

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: He had further supplementary que stions. He had not  at any point
indicated to you that he ha d finished. Are you now sayi ng that if you do not like
something that is going to happen, you are just going to discontinue the question and
move on? That is wrong.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, the member is quite right—that  is exactly what I am saying. If
we are going to get into a situation—[ Interruption] Order! If we are going to get into a
situation where I detect that a member is creating disorder, then I will move on. On this
occasion I will allow David Parker to finish his supplementary questions.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. You said in your
ruling that you had relied upon a previous Spea ker’s ruling. Can you tell us what that
ruling is, please.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, I did not say I had relied on a previous Speaker’s ruling. I said I
had given a very substantive ruling some 2 or 3 months ago. I will send a copy to the
member so he is fully aware of it.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. I am sorry. If I can just
make it clear, it was a previous ruling of the current Speaker, not a ruling of the
previous Speaker, that the Speaker was referring to.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And that is not a point of order.  I have allowed David Parker to
continue with his line of questioning.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Given the Minister of Fina nce’s statement on Monday about
Labour’s criticism of his Gove rnment around Solid Energy and the Future Investment
Fund, when he said “They need to show us who they’re go ing to borrow the money off,
which foreign bankers are going to lend us the money.”, if his Government provides a
loan to Solid Energy that is not from the Future Investment Fund, will the Government
borrow for the loan, or is he just going to print the money?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Just as with student loans, we will be borrowing for it.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Which is correct: that Treasury officials made a mistake reading
the Cabinet minutes and appropriated $100 milli on from assets sale proceeds to “Solid

Better Public Services Targets—Advanced Trade Qualifications, Diplomas, and
Degrees
8. TIM MACINDOE (National—Hamilton West)  to the Minister for Tertiary
Education, Skills and Employment : What progress has the Government made on its
Better Public Services target of increasi ng the proportion of 25-34 year olds with a
Level 4 or above qualification?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for T ertiary Education, Skills and
Employment): Very good progress indeed. In 2012, 52.6 percent of all 25 to 34-year-
olds had achieved an advanced trade qualif ication, diploma, or degree at level 4 or
above on the New Zealand Qua lifications Framework. This is up from 51.8 percent in
2011. That means over 8,100 more 25 to 34-year-old s gained qualifications at level 4 or
above last year than in the previous year. The Government is working very hard to meet
its target of 55 percent by 2017.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: What signals indicate the Government is on track to meet its target?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, for this target the num ber of 22-year-olds achieving
level 4 or above qualifications is a very important indicator for the progress towards the
overall target of 55 percent. That is becau se, of course, people who were 22 last year
will turn 25 in 3 years’ time. In 2012, 34 percent of 22-year-olds had completed a
qualification at level 4 and a bove in that year. That comp ares with 30 percent 4 years
ago, in 2008, so that is encouraging progress. I am particularly pleased with the increase
in achievement for M āori and Pasifika students. In 2012, 22 percent of M āori 22-year-
olds achieved a qualification at level 4 a nd above, compared with 15 percent 4 years
ago, in 2008. In regards to Pasi fika, 26 percent of 22-year-old Pasifika students in 2012
had completed a qualification, compared w ith only 14 percent in 2008. So we are not
there yet, but we are making very good progress.
10 Jul 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 11853

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: Why is the Government focusing on increasing the number of 25 to
34-year-olds with a level 4 or above qualification?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: For several reasons: firstly, level 4 qualifications are the
minimum standard of competency for many vocational occupations, and increasing the
number of people with level 4 or above qualifications increases the skill levels in New
Zealand workplaces and contributes to  economic growth. A level 4 or above
qualification also has a significant impact on an individual’s income for them and, of
course, for supporting their family. For exampl e, the median weekly income for 25 to
34-year-olds in 2011, when they had level 4 to 7 vocational qualifications, was $106
more a week than for 25 to 34-year-olds w ithout those qualifications. And, of course, a
higher-level qualification also means people tend to be employed, stay employed, and
spend less time on the unemployment benefit than those who do not have qualifications.

9. JACINDA ARDERN (Labour)  to the Minister for Social Development : Does

Better Public Services Targets—Reduction in Reoffending
10. IAN McKELVIE (National—Rangit īkei) to the Minister of Corrections :
What progress has the Government made on its target of reducing re-offending by 25
percent by 2017?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I am pleased to advise the House
that Better Public Services re sults released this week show that reoffending rates are
down 9 percent since June 2011. There are al so more prisoners than ever before
involved in drug and alcohol rehabilitation, employment  training, and education
programmes. These results are very encourag ing and show that the initiatives this
Government is rolling out across the Department of Corrections are having a real impact
on reoffending rates and are making our communities safer. To put these figures in
perspective, a 9 percent re duction in reoffending mean s there are over 1,600 fewer
offenders and 6,600 fewer victims.

items.speaker: Ian McKelvie
items.text: What further initiatives is the Government rolling out to improve
offender rehabilitation?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: This Government is determined to deliver programmes that
address the drivers of crime: addiction, lack  of employment skills, and poor education.
As part of the reducing reoffending programme, every year we will be providing alcohol
and drug treatment to 33,100 additional offende rs and numeracy and literacy training to
an additional 1,200 prisoners. To increase employment training, the Government is
establishing full working prisons at Au ckland Women’s Pris on, Tongariro/Rangip ō
Prison, and Rolleston Prison. As part of this initiative work is under way to construct a
building yard at Rolleston Prison, which will see prisoners repair 150 State houses from
the red zone over the next 5 years. Pris oners will, of course, be provided with
construction skills and qualifications that will help them find employment in the
Christchurch rebuild on their release.

items.speaker: Ian McKelvie
items.text: What is the Government doing to  reduce the chances of a prisoner
reoffending following their release from prison?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Prisoners are at a high risk of  returning to crime as soon as
they are released from prison. Around 50 percen t of prisoners are back in prison within
4 years. In addition to the increased reha bilitation that we ar e providing in prison,
Budget 2013 made $10 million available from th e justice sector fund to establish the
11856 Questions for Oral Answer 10 Jul 2013
new Out of Gate reintegrati on programme. This new nati onwide post-release service
will see prisoners supported as soon as th ey leave a facility. Up to 4,000 prisoners
serving a sentence of less than 2 years will be allocated a dedicated provider who will
connect them to social services and help with accommodation, employment, and general
living skills.

“Corporal Jones”. “Corporal J ones” appears, yelling: “Don ’t panic. Don’t panic. The
Germans are coming. Don’t panic.” John Key sits calmly and says: “I normally get my
list of overseas migrants. Where are the Aust ralians? Where are the Indians? Where are
the Chinese? I am being told only about the Germans.”
In John Key’s Helensville it is Dad’s Army all over the place. Well, on this side of
the House, we say: “Who are you kidding, Mr Key?”. He tells us he cannot remember a
very large multimillionaire—

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Billionaire.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: —multibillionaire—German arriving in his electorate. He
says that he cannot remember the man who put  on the biggest fireworks display in New
Zealand’s history. But he does not know, because he is surrounded by his Dad’s Army
of advisers. John Key is surrounded by Steven  Joyce as Corporal Jones. “He doesn’t
like it up ‘em.”, as he woul d say. “He doesn’t lik e it up ‘em.” That is what Corporal
Jones would tell the House.
But, you see, what John Key tells us is th at he has a mandate to govern. Well, it is
certainly true that John Key ha s been on a hell of a lot of man dates. He went on a man
date with John Banks, and he got a seat in Parliament. He went on a man date with Ian
Fletcher, and he got a job r unning the Government Communications Security Bureau.
He went on a man date with the Skycity ch ief executives, and they got a whole law for
themselves. Man dates are what John Key doe s, but someone else always wins out of
them other than New Zealanders.
10 Jul 2013 General Debate 11859
People who are associating themselves with  John Key have another problem. Those
who go on man dates with John Key have a major problem: “PTD ”, or politically
transmitted diseases—politically transmitted diseases. Every time anyone goes near
him, there is trouble. John Banks cannot ev en remember what day it is. He does not
even know where he is. He cannot reme mber $50,000 worth of donations from the
German in the mansion. Peter Dunne has comp letely lost his way—totally discredited.
And the M āori Party appears to have three leader s, or it might have two, and certainly
after the next election it will have one or none  at all. So politically transmitted diseases
are the order of the day for anyone who comes into contact with John Key.
But on a serious note, tomorrow this House will debate the Skycity law—the “Casino
Bill”—and there is nothing that is more of an  emblem of this Government than that bill.
It is a convention centre built off the back of problem gamblers; a convention centre that
will add 8,000 additional problem gamblers; a convention centre built with a dodgy
process, where the Prime Mini ster intervened; a convention centre built by selling off
the laws of this country; and a convention ce ntre that typifies a Government that works
for vested interests and not in the interest s of New Zealanders. This Government is a
crony capitalist Government.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, we know
what Grant Robertson was doing last night. In between his desperate denials on Twitter,
he was watching the JONES! channel. That wa s the inspiration for his speech today. It
was his JONES! channel. The only thing is that he should have been Sergeant Schultz
today, because he is the one running around saying “I see nothing. I know nothing.
There’s nobody challenging for the leadership  of the Labour Party. I know nothing at
all.”, when the reality is that there is a Jones channel, and the Jones channel is the
channel by which the leadership challenge of the Labour Party is being conducted.
It has been a fascinating 24 hours in the identity politics of the Labour Party. First,
we had the man ban, then we had the ban of the man ban, and then, very nearly, we had
the demise of the man who banned the man ban. That is where it nearly got to last night,
and it is where it is heading again t oday. Despite the denials—the many, many
denials—the reality is that there are three of the men who were go ing to be banned in
the man ban who have decided to take their opportunity and step forward. I say stand up
those men who are against the man ban—Sha ne Jones, Andrew Little, and Clayton
Cosgrove—the red meat men of the Labour  Party, who are, as we speak, either
circulating or not circulating, or denying they are circulating, a letter of no confidence in
the leadership of the Labour Party. That is what is going on right now. The red meat
division has decided that this is its chance to get its own back.
But those members did not quite succeed. A ll they succeeded in doing yesterday was
causing a massive Twitter explosion last night. There was a massive explosion on
Twitter, where nearly all the Labour Party caucus, except Shane Jones, except Andrew
Little, except Clayton Cosgr ove, and except a bunch of ot her Labour Party members,
were on Twitter last night saying “No, ther e’s nothing happening here.”, and Annette
King was even on the radio this morning sa ying: “No, there’s nothing happening here.”
Well, you know what you say about denials. “De Niles” is a river in Egypt, and the
reality of the situation is that the Labour Party is heading towards a leadership revolt.
Mr Shearer, of course, is desperately tryi ng to shore up his lead ership, and today he
has made a significant bid in that regard. He  has decided that the vote for jobs and
growth tomorrow will be a conscience vote for his caucus, and he welcomes people who
want to vote for the New Zealand International Convention Centre to do so tomorrow.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: That was the Speaker’s ruling.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Speaker has ruled—abs olutely right—but go and
check. There has been a statement released by your leader this afternoon, where he has
11860 General Debate 10 Jul 2013
said that if members of his caucus want to vote in favour of the convention centre
tomorrow, they are welcome to do so. Of course, most of them will not be voting in
favour, but it will be interesting to see who does,  and I think it is yet another test of this
man’s leadership.
On this side of the House it is pretty clear. On this side of the House we are in favour
of jobs and growth for New Zealanders. Ev ery day this Government proves that, and
tomorrow is just another day when we prove that we are in favour of jobs and growth
for New Zealanders. But not the modern Labour Pa rty. It used to be like that. It actually
supported a convention centre be ing built in a very simila r arrangement 10 years ago,
but not today—not today. Those members are caught up in identity politics and are
focusing on the man ban. Well, tomorrow a few of them—the few middle-of-the-
roaders left—have an opportunity to stand up and say: “Actually, no. We are in favour
of jobs and growth, and we should go forward and say so.”
There are three or four of them who might  do that. Obviously, th ey would then have
to turn their backs on Grant Robertson and David Parker, and so on. But, for example,
the “fab four” who attended the Eden Park discussion with Skycity in the corporate
box—[Interruption]—or was it six, or was it eight— will have the opportunity to do so,
and we will know whether there is anybody left  in the Labour Party who supports jobs
and growth or not. So tomorrow is a test of Labour Party caucus members. It is yet
another day of a test of the Labour Party leadership—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: This is a very long 5 minutes, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: —and I will finish by saying th at I thought that in the
audition for Mr Grant Roberts on just now, he got more la ughs in 5 minutes than his
leader has had in 18 months.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: I want to start off my contribution this
afternoon by thanking you, Mr Speaker, for th e decision to hold a conscience vote on
the Skycity bill tomorrow. I am distressed to hear the way that the National member
Steven Joyce has treated the issue of consci ence votes. When it has been agreed that a
conscience vote should be held, it is the ri ght of each individual member to make the
decision for themselves. It may well be that  most members from a particular party
decide to vote the way that their leader believes they ought to vote. There are lots of
reasons why that may be the case. The nature of the vote and the fact of the vote are of
less consequence than the right of each indi vidual member to vote according to their
conscience. That is the right that members have when the Speaker makes a decision as
he has done.
This means that Auckland now has the ability  to take real action on the Skycity deal
as well. Auckland people who are opposed to  this deal now have  a genuine opportunity
to speak to their local representative, fr om whichever party, and say to their local
representative: “We believe that this deal should not procee d, and we would like you to
represent our views when you vote tomorrow on th is bill.” It is a genuine reflection of
the democracy that allows the members of the public who are most affected by this
issue—that is, those who live in Auck land—to talk with their MPs, their
representatives, in a genuine  way, to say: “We would lik e you to vote like this.” The
Speaker has given those MPs the opportunity to reflect their constituents’ views—their
constituents’ views. For that we are very grateful, and we would like to see this continue
through the whole process of this bill. Thank you, Mr Speaker.
Actually, my contribution today was intende d to be not so much  on Skycity but on
the issues of gender, because the National Part y has such a poor leve l of representation
of women in Parliament. [ Interruption] I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. It is very
difficult to continue my speech with the c onversation that is be ing shouted across from
one side of me to the other.
10 Jul 2013 General Debate 11861

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Would members cease the interjecti ons, because it is distracting to
the member who is speaking.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Thank you. Why is the National Party lagging so far behind
when it comes to women’s representation? Last term, 29 percent of its caucus were
women; this term it is 25 percent—one in four. It is lagging behind. Do you know what
we heard from the National Government’s Mi nister of Women’s Affairs, Jo Goodhew?
Do you know what she told Morning Report  just this week—on Friday, actually?
People should be selected on merit alone, sa id the Minister of Women’s Affairs. She
said that New Zealand had a proud history of women succeeding on the basis of their
competency. Is Minister Goodhew really sayi ng that of all the women in the National
Party, only 25 percent are comp etent enough to be MPs? Is that what she is really
saying? Does her att itude explain why it is that the Government has this miserable
target for the private sector boards of havi ng only 10 percent of private sector boards
being women? Is that because the National Government’s Minister of Women’s Affairs
believes that only 10 percent of women who are in business are competent enough to be
on these boards? In terms of partners in law firms, an area partic ularly special to my
heart, only 16 percent of women lawyers are partners. Does Jo Goodhew believe that
only 16 percent of women lawyers are competent to be partners in law firms?
The Green Party is very proud of its record  of having a majority of women in our
caucus represented in this Parliament, because  we believe that representation of women
is absolutely critical. We believe that wome n do have all the skills and capacity to be
representatives in this House, for this House to be genuinely a representative
democracy, and we make sure it is possibl e—we make sure it is possible—unlike the
National Party, which is actively, obviousl y, excluding women from the opportunity to
hold positions of authority in its party. There is no commitment in the National Party to
any kind of representative democracy. It pr efers a male-dominated elite to be making
decisions and to be sucking resources to th at male-dominated elite, and leaving women,
leaving their children, and leaving all of thos e others who are entitled to be represented
here out in the cold. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: What a joy to follow the lecture
that we have just received from that member, Metiria Turei. Oh, for goodness’ sake!
Honestly, I was so, so enthralled with her lectur e that I almost forgot  that last night she
was so busy lecturing us that she forgot to vote against the legal assistance legislation
that she had railed against from one end of th e country to the other. It was wonderful to
have her support in the final moments, so  that, in fact, the bills went through
unanimously. So well done, Ms Turei, well done—you are finally seeing some sense.
But I have to say that that presentati on on merit and how bad it is was pretty
amazing. To say that over here the women ar e—what? We are dominated by the men? I
think that is a bit of a joke. Unfortunately, what I can see, though, is that in the Labour
Party, of course, it is, in fact, all about the man ban. Why is it that with the three
different factions in the Labour  Party all vying to take th e leadership, not one of the
leaders or deputy leaders in contention is a woman? Why is that? Of course, the reason
is that they are always chosen on merit. That is why it is; it is clearly on merit.
I thought Ms Moroney did brilliantly on The Nation  last weekend. I am looking
forward to her coming on again next weekend, and probably Q+A, as well. It was so
much fun, I even taped it. It was fantastic. I played it again just in case some people
missed it—and they really should see it. I ha ve no idea why she is not allowed to turn
up in the media more often. It must be because she is a woman! That is what it is in the
Labour Party. That must be the reason.
But, of course, David—what is hi s name? David Shearer yesterday—
[Interruption]—well, that is what they asked on Morning Report yesterday on Radio
11862 General Debate 10 Jul 2013

items.speaker: New Zealand National. They said
items.text: “Where is David Shearer?”, because for the first time
in living memory, I think since the 1930s, wh en the Labour Party was first set up, a
Labour Party leader refused to go on Morning Report . How does that happen? How
does that happen? He refused to go on beca use he did not want to talk about Ms
Moroney’s very good attempt to bring in the man ban. It is so clearly needed because
Labour has only two women on its front bench, and, of course , we have got three. Of
course, our three are equal to about six of th em when it comes to merit. But having said
that, why is it?
All the last week we have watched as  the Labour Party has imploded and it has
talked about the things that nobody cares a bout—in other words, getting rid of men, not
letting them compete equally against wome n, and turning them into an endangered
species, if they were not already within the Labour Party.
But, of course, what have we been doing? Well, we have had a bit of fun, I have to
say, amongst all the work, and most of that fun has been at the expense of Labour
members. But we have also been getting on with the job of government, thinking about
what it is that the people of New Zealand want. They want jobs. There is the convention
centre deal, which I am sure those peopl e in the Labour Party probably will end up
voting for. I am sure that Phil Goff, Cl ayton Cosgrove, David Shearer—and who else—
Annette King, and Kris Faafoi will want to  vote for the convention centre legislation.
They were very happy to take the hospita lity of Skycity the other week—why was
that—after they had been bagging them day i n, day out in the media. Of course, what
they did was stay there all night, just to te ll them off. It is amazing what those poor
people endured.
We are also into bringing the crime rate  down, and this last week we announced our
Better Public Services targets. What can we  say? Under Labour, pr isons got full. Under
National, crime is coming down. Youth cr ime has dropped 18 percent since June
2011—a fantastic rate. Total crime is down 11 percent. Reoffending is down 9 percent.
Under Labour, what was happening? Violen t crime was going up, and reoffending was
going up. Labour made no progress. Poor Miss Mo roney is still trying to get a question
in the House. Why can that woman not get a que stion? Why is that? It is because she is
not on merit—no, she is on merit.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: The woman has a name.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: She has, and she deserves it, because she has helped us in
Hamilton West to make it a safe National seat, and before that she did the same for
Hamilton East. I think that is an outstand ing record, and I am looking forward to her
doing it again in Christchurch East, because apparently it is that member whom the
hierarchy want to be there. That, of course , will be on merit—yes, absolutely. I see the
Tui billboard coming on.
I am so proud to be a member of this Na tional-led Government. It is working well
and getting on with the business. It is talki ng about the stuff peopl e want. What we are
doing is we are getting the crime rate dow n, getting jobs for people, bringing the
economy further up, and actually undoing some of the rot that Labour left us with.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: That was an intriguing speech from Judith Collins,
a woman who has a Twitter account that 99 percent of people assume is a parody
because it is so bizarre and so random. I take offence at her lecturing Metiria Turei
about the merits of women, after she tweeted  last week: “What a vile, vulgar, ugly
speech Metiria Turei gave, just like her jack et.”—just like her jacket. How is that being
a role model for women in this House, when  apparently the jacket that a woman wears
is more important than the substance of the speeches that she gives in this House?
I want to inform the New Zealand public that that Twitter account is not a parody; it
is real. That is how scary it is . She actually believes those th ings that she is saying on
10 Jul 2013 General Debate 11863
that account. I think that Ms Collins is on wafer-thin ice when sh e lectures anyone on
this side of the House on the merits of women and respecting the role of women in
Parliament.
It has been interesting to see the focus of  the National Party. One of the issues we
want to talk about on this si de of the House is power pric es. In 1 year disconnections
have jumped by 10,000. Mr Simon Bridges, the Minister of Energy and Resources, said:
“There’s no problem. Nothing to see here. Th at’s OK.” Power prices  have continued to
increase at double the rate of inflation, desp ite flattening demand, despite the surplus of
supply, and despite a collapsed  carbon price, and Minister  Bridges says: “That’s OK.
It’s all fine. Nothing to see here.”
It is unfortunate that it has been left to Simon Bridges to deal with this issue, because
he is the Justin Bieber of the National Cabine t. He does not take th ese issues seriously.
What he has been saying cons istently is that power prices  are not too high. We said to
him: “Well, then, what would be too hi gh?”. He replied: “Oh, I don’t know—I don’t
know.” That is not an appropriate answer from a Minister of Energy and Resources who
is overseeing a jump in disconnections of  10,000. People cannot have power connected
over winter because they cannot afford to pay the power bills, and the National
Government has no plan to do anything about that.
I suspect that Minister Bridges would thi nk that power prices were too high if he
could not afford to pay the power bill. I susp ect that that is the real answer to that
question. National members will think power prices are too high when the massive tax
cut they gave themselves is no longer enough to pay the power bill. But the unfortunate
reality out there for most punters is that as winter kicks in and as power bills are landing
in letterboxes, family budgets are being st ressed, and the National Party is saying:
“There is no problem. There is nothing to see here. Please look the other way, because
that is certainly what we are doing.”
One of the most extraordinary statements fr om Minister Bridges was: “Well, we just
haven’t given the Bradford reforms enough time to bed in.” Given th at he was not even
born when they first came in, I do not know how  long he needs to show that they have
utterly and completely failed to deliver th e competition and the price reductions that
were promised at that time. They have fa iled. They have not worked. They do not need
time to bed in. They need to be reformed. Th ey need to be changed. Tinkering will not
help. A Labour Government is the only Government that is going to be prepared to do
that.
Minister Bridges’ answer to this is al ways: “We have this fantastic What’s My
Number campaign, so the fact that people are able to switch power companies and go
and find out all the different opt ions proves that there’s compet ition.” Firstly, if there is
such great competition in the market, why do we need to throw millions of dollars at a
What’s My Number campaign, in order to improve competition? But, more important,
what does that programme do for the poorest families in this country?

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Nothing.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Nothing. Do you know why? Because the families that I am
dealing with every single day at home, who cannot pay their power bills, are lucky if
they can find one power company to pick them up. The idea that they could have a
choice of power company—[Interruption] Anne Tolley, who has moved from Gisborne
to Ōhope Beach and so is hardly ever in Gisb orne now, does not realise, perhaps, just
how hard people are doing it in Gisborne. The local fire service tells me that it is seeing
an increase in house fires because of peopl e using little gas stoves to cook on and
candles to light their homes. Maybe she needs to spend a little bit more time in
Gisborne, to get some idea of how hard people are doing it there.
11864 General Debate 10 Jul 2013
The reality is that most families in that  position cannot find one power company to
take them on. So when they hear the Nati onal Party and Anne Tolley lecturing them,
saying: “Well, just change power companies. You have a choice.”, they realise just how
out of touch this National Government is . Those programmes do not help the poorest
families. Simon Bridges, the Minister, does not care about those families—neither does
this Government—and that is why the La bour-Greens NZ Power policy is the only
policy that is going to deliver for the poorest families in New Zealand.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: It is a complete joke for
that member, Moana Mackey, to be lecturing the National Government on power prices,
because the Government that she was a part of raised power prices from 1999 to 2008
by 72 percent. So if she is complaining about the price now, that is because power
prices went up under her Government. Under th is Government, power prices have gone
up by only 16 percent. So when Labour members say that they have got the answer on
power prices, they know that they are dead wrong. Quite frankly, there is a word for that
beginning with “h” that would describe anything they say about electricity prices.
Those people over there are truly the unelect ables. There is no question about that.
When you look at the options once David Shearer  goes, it is not a very pretty sight.
Grant Robertson was doing his leadership audition here today, and I must say that it was
not too bad, really, if you wanted a light comedy routine. But when you team him up
with Andrew Little and Shane Jones, you ha ve got three guys—two of whom cannot
win an electorate seat and the other one is completely unelectable as the leader. So I
reckon that although they might be happy individually, they are in a pretty bad space.
What I think is really disgraceful is the wa y that they are acting towards their leader.
If that Twitter explosion from last night was not treachery at its worst—and if those
denials do not actually signa l that the coup is on—I do  not know what is. Grant
Robertson is pretty happy because he has convi nced David Shearer that he is allowed to
answer only one question each day. That is why, 37 times since he was elected leader,
David Shearer has come into this House and said: “Prime Minister, do you stand by all
your statements?” or “Does he stand by all his statements?”. That is the one question
that David Shearer asks every day, and the rest of the time he is totally dazed and
confused.
I think that the Labour research unit is pulling David Shearer’s chain. It is conning
him completely, because, quite frankly, it is  not giving him a fair go. Grant Robertson
there is not supporting his leader. He ca nnot wait for David Shearer to go. David
Cunliffe was up there today having a go. Wh o else was there? There was the other
fellow—Shane Jones. Shane Jones is suddenly back in the game because he knows that
the coup is coming and it is all going to be  up for grabs. Even Darren Hughes’ landlady
might fancy herself as making a bit of a comeback. It could be  anyone. The good news
is that they are all completely unelectable, so it is good times ahead.
The one man they do really want to ban is David Shearer. They want to get rid of this
guy, but there is no one there with the steel a nd the political nerve to actually grasp the
chalice. If Grant Robertson was up to it, he would never have let Shearer get that job in
the first place. That is the fact of it. Grant cannot do the job. Old what’s-his-name Shane
Jones is not up to it either. He had his chan ce. So, really, there is  not the next Labour
Prime Minister in Parliament at this stage, and that is a very big problem.
Tomorrow we are going to be voting on the Skycity Casino legislation. That is going
to be a conscience vote, and I am looking fo rward to Phil Goff, Kris Faafoi, Clayton
Cosgrove, and David Shearer a ll voting for it because they w ould not want to look like
hypocrites.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: Annette King.
10 Jul 2013 General Debate 11865

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Oh, and Annette Kin g. You would look like a
bit of a hypocrite if you went to the Skycity box, if you drank all night, and if you ate all
night, and you came in here and voted against the legislation—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. I was in the Chamber last
night when the Chairman of the Committee ruled against the use of the word
“hypocrite”. I am surprised th at you did not pull the member up, particularly as I could
have thrown that back at him as a member  who went to a corpor ate box with a tobacco
company—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! The member is quite right. The word
should not have been used, and I ask the Minister to stand a nd withdraw the use of that
word.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I withdraw, but I think you get the gist of what
is going on. So, anyway, those guys over there—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. He cannot then comment on
your ruling.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That is true. Would the member, now that he has withdrawn that
comment, just continue his speech.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I withdraw. But, as I was saying, those four
Labour members were at the Skycity box, so, of  course, morally, they are compelled to
vote for the legislation tomorrow, because Annette King is for jobs and growth, and Phil
Goff is for jobs and growth. Grant Robert son is not, and he is the only option Labour
has got as the leader for the future. The more it gets bogged down in things like the man
ban, the less it is able to connect with the people of New Zealand.
I can tell you a story. A lady I know in Auckland, a friend of my family, had a couple
of plumbers around last week, and they said : “Well, I guess it’s the last you’ll be seeing
of us.” She said: “Why?”. They said: “Well, the way it’s going, if Labour ever gets into
Government, we’ll have to send only female plumbers here.” The point of this story is
that once the plumbers and the blokes driv ing the white vans are getting the message
that the guys over there are against the “blokey tradies”, as Shane Jones calls them,
those guys have lost. So I think that with the man ban thing, Labour has conscribed
itself to the wilderness for a decade, I would say. It is looking pretty bad for Labour.
Meanwhile, over here, we are focusing on the economy—the best economic growth
in the OECD bar Australia—the jobless rate being down, inflation being down, and
good economic times. We are looking very good. Those guys there are absolutely
hopeless.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR (NZ First) : Honourable members,
today I want to talk about an issue of concern.

items.speaker: Paul Foster-Bell
items.text: What’s that?
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR : That issue is crime, Mr Foster-Bell.
We are all very aware that some of our c itizens fail to behave in accordance with the
law. So New Zealand, like every society, has to live with a certain amount of illegal and
dysfunctional behaviour. Human perfection is not likely to happen any time soon.
Accordingly, our society must be able to marshal such levers as will influence people to
abide by the law. These points need to be made because right now in New Zealand it is
plain that many of those who break the law in a serious way are getting an uncertain
message about how unacceptable their behaviour is to law-abiding society.
Let me mention a few recent examples. Darren Murphy Fidow, age 18, brutally
attacked an 82-year-old woman. He was sent enced to only 11 months’ home detention.
John Richard Cox received 6 months’ home de tention and 150 hours’ community work
for making incorrect tax claims for his clients without their knowledge, which amounted
to a fraud of well over $400,000. Eru Michael Timoti, 27, a factory worker, had sex
11866 General Debate 10 Jul 2013
with an under-age girl for over a year, knowing that it was illegal. He was sentenced to
200 hours’ community work and 18 months’ intensive supervision.
It would be inappropriate for me to comment  in detail on any specific criminal case,
but what is apparent is a clear pattern of extremely serious crime resulting in sentences
that would strike most New Zealanders as lenient—as lenient. Justice must be done, and
it must be seen to be done. We place gr eat trust in our judiciary—we do. Those
appointed to the judiciary in New Zealand are people of the highest calibre—the highest
calibre. But, ultimately, if people believe that sentences do not reflect the harm that
individuals in society have suffered, conf idence in the whole judicial process will
suffer.
Has the Government directed judges to av oid prison sentences because of the cost
and serious overcrowding? That is a good question for the Minister of Justice to answer.
The public are rightly concerned about what appear to be lenient sentences, and they are
questioning the validity of our court syst em. The public can be forgiven for their
scepticism. They can be forgiven. Is some thing going on here? What are we not being
told? Is lenient sentencing a covert way of saving money? Is leniency an undeclared
way of keeping prison populations down? Is it? What we do know is that the public take
crime very, very seriously. New Zealand Fi rst takes crime very, very seriously. In
relation to crime, we must all stand together—we must.
Earlier this week we watched in horror a chase on television. The chase started in
Ōpōtiki and went all the way up to North Auckland. That chase took over 3 hours and
shut down the motorway for 14 hours.

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: How many?
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR : 14 hours, Mr Banks. Do you
remember something now? New Zealand Fi rst wants to commend the New Zealand
Police for its handling of the extremely dangero us situation. But it does raise yet more
concerns—it does raise more concerns. Let me put it in plain language: it means that the
Minister is asleep at the wheel—it does.

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: Speak up.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR: I am speaking up for that, as you can
hear. You cannot even remember half of the story, Mr Banks.
It means our police force is under-resour ced. It means our community safety is
hugely compromised. It means the Minister an d the Government are turning a blind eye
to the huge number of unrepor ted incidents and unrecorded crimes. There are just not
enough police—there are just not enough po lice—to cope with the demand. The
Government should stop boasting about the crime rate coming down, because we have
got prisons overflowing with prisoners. New Zealand still has one of the highest rates of
incarceration in the world. How can our prisons be overflowing if the crime rate is
coming down? How can you expect the prisons—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I apologise for interrupting th e member. The member’s time has
expired.

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: What a soul-destroying rant from the list
member from the “New Zealand First, Winston Second Party”.
Why is the Leader of the Opposition not here this afternoon?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: OK, I will not, Mr Speaker. The Leader of the Opposition
needs to get up in the House and take calls like this to defend his position. It seems to be
that I have never seen a Labour Party in such disarray. In 10 Parliaments of being here, I
have never seen a more dejected, redu ced-to-nothing, hopelessly out-of-control,
miserable specimen of an individual than the leader of the Labour Party. Why is it that
his bench mate Grant Robertson, “The Toad fr om Toad Hall”, looks so happy? In the A
10 Jul 2013 General Debate 11867
A Milne book Toad of Toad Hall, Toad of Toad Hall looks so happy. He looks so happy
because he is creative and he is devious, but he is self-centred to the point of
sociopathy. He is self-centred. The “member for Vivian Street” is happy today because
he wants to take over the man tle of the leadership—the remnants of the leadership—of
the Labour Party. But he is completely lacking in common sense.
Toad of Toad Hall is known as someone who is always clever, devious, educated—
over-educated—and over-competent, but lacki ng common sense. That over there is
“The Toad from Toad Hall”, who would be th e leader of the Labour  Party if the poor
joker—to use the vernacular, the Leader of the Opposition has just finished a long visit
to the taxidermist. He is finished. It is al l over. I have never seen  anyone so dejected. I
have never seen anyone so miserable. He sits there at question time, he eats peanuts, he
chews his fingernails, he feels out of depth, and all he is saying is: “If only I were in
New York with my secret bank account, it woul d be so much better than this place of
purgatory.” But “The Toad from Toad Hall”, the grunter from Vivian Street, is there. He
is ready to take over, and he would be an equal disaster.
In A A Milne’s book it says: “When the Toad came down the street howling, the
streets were full of people jeer ing at the sight.” That is what will happen with that
leader. So we get rid of the hapless Mr Sh earer, and we get the “member for Vivian
Street” in charge of the Labour Party. That is where Labour  members belong—in
Opposition for a long, long time. They can have their Moët champagne at Skycity; they
can have their secret bank accounts in New Yo rk; they can have their hapless, hopeless,
and useless leaders; and they can have their very earnest little chief Government whips.
But what they cannot have is any const ituency out there that represents common
ground, common sense, investment, growth, or jobs. The Labour Party is in a bad way.
A day before I entered Parliament in 1981 there were four women members of
Parliament. The day after I entered Parlia ment, 10 Parliaments ago, there were eight
women members of Parliament. Today ther e are 44 women members of Parliament.
What we need are high-quality women me mbers of Parliament, like the two I am
looking at now and the one who is behind me —the three on this side of the House—
Mrs Tolley, Mrs Upston, and this lovely member over here.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Tell us her name.

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: What is wrong with that? On their own, those three women
would be an Opposition demolition team, and they would not need “The Toad from
Toad Hall”, the “member for Vivian Street”.
Is it going to be Shearer, Robertson, Cunliffe, or Little? We on this side of the House
do not care, as long as they stay where they are. As long as no one cares, because no one
up and down the country cares, this Labour Party is in disarray from the grassroots up.
Worse, by cuddling up to the Greens, Labour  has become a party intent on destroying
business, growth, and jobs, and more content on  staying over there, and that is not all
bad.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: When Mr Banks gets back to his office,
he can reflect on where he went wrong with that speech. He went  wrong right at the
point that he decided to introduce Parliament  to the women on the National side of the
House. He got two out of three, and he coul d not remember the name of the third one.
At that point it went wrong fo r Mr Banks. We know that his memory is not particularly
good.
John Banks could not remember being flown in Kim Dotcom’s personal helicopter to
his mansion, where he met the giraffe a nd got given $50,000. The same man put on a
fireworks display for Auckland, but John Ba nks could not remember. Kim Dotcom is
the guy who put on the biggest fireworks di splay Auckland has ever seen. John Banks
sent him a note to say thank you, and then claimed he could not remember. And he
11868 General Debate 10 Jul 2013
could not remember Melissa Lee’s name when  he was speaking. That is the point at
which his speech all started to go very, very wrong.
If I were John Banks, I woul d not be talking about secr et bank accounts or Skycity.
Bear in mind that John Banks is the man who pretended not to know that Skycity gave a
massive contribution to his campaign. He said  he did not know about it, even though
they personally handed him the cheque. We ll, I do not know about you, but if someone
gives me a cheque for $15,000, I generally tend to remember that. That is not the sort of
thing I would forget.
Who else have we had from National toda y? Well, we have had the great Mount
Albert maestro, Jonathan Coleman. Jonathan Coleman—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: He wishes he could forget things.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: He wishes he could forget things. He wishes he could forget the
Mt Albert by-election. Jonathan Coleman deci ded to give us a lecture on corporate box
etiquette. When Jonathan Young was the O pposition spokesperson on health, he took
money from the tobacco industry and decided to  blow smoke in their faces in their own
corporate box. Who else did we have? Well, we had Judith Collins. “Cruella” herself
decided to make a contribution. I want to know why Judith Collins had to speak after
Steven Joyce. Has the deal already been  done? Has the succession planning already
been mapped out for the National Party?
The deal has been done. We know that J ohn Key does not want to stick around after
the next election, so has the deal been done? Yes,  they have stitched it up. It is going to
be “Corporate Jones”, Steven Joyce, and “Cruella”, with the Dalmatians lined up behind
them. That is the deal. It is another deal that National has done behind closed doors, a
lot like all of the other ones that John Key is so keen on doing.
John Key cannot sit down for a meal without whacking New Zealanders with another
massive bill. Every time that man sits dow n for a meal, New Zealanders end up paying.
He sits down with Warner Bros, and there is a law change that they pay for. He sits
down with John Banks—another dodgy deal—w ith Peter Dunne, with Skycity. Every
time John Key meets somebody, he does another dodgy deal.
I found it very ironic that Jonathan Coleman decided to  ask why it was that David
Shearer always asks John Key whether he stands by all of his statements. [ Interruption]
Well, I will answer that for Jonathan Cole man. It is because for the first time in New
Zealand’s history we have a Prime Minister who has to think about it. He actually has to
pause and think about it: “Oh my goodness, what  did I say? What did I say?”. He has to
think about it.
I found this comment from John Key very, ve ry revealing, when he was talking
about his relationship with the parliamentar y press gallery. He said: “I’ve found in my
time as Prime Minister I’ve had less engagement with the press gallery simply because I
do not mislead people, so I have  to answer the que stion if they ask me a question.” So
his solution to dealing with the press gallery is that he does not want to mislead them, so
he just does not talk to them. He just avoi ds the question in the first place because he
does not want to get caught out not telling the truth, which has happened so many times
before.
This is a Government that is simply in tent on doing all of the dodgy deals that
advantage its mates. It is not interested in the issues that hard-working New Zealand
families care about. Power prices are going up all the time, and this Government says it
does not have a problem with that. It th inks the power prices  are right for the
environment—that is what National says. Actually, New Zealanders are saying that they
do not think that is right. This is a Govern ment that wants to take hundreds of millions
of dollars a year out of the electricity i ndustry—out of Transpower, in particular—in
10 Jul 2013 General Debate 11869
dividends and force New Zealanders to overpay for their power. This is not a
Government that is concerned about the issues affecting ordinary New Zealanders.

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: One would have to stand in the House this
week and ask what the most important i ssues are for hard-working Kiwis. Well,
according to the Labour Party, it is whet her or not its caucus of—how many—33 has
enough women, or, actually, whether there are t oo many men. That is the issue that it
has been talking about day af ter day after day. And you know what? It could not even
count. It could not even count the number  of women it has now, so good luck with
getting to your 45 or 50 percent—I hope you can count by then.
Let us actually quote from one of its own. Josie Pagani, who was a candidate for the
Labour Party, says that Labour is “stuck  talking about ‘man-bans’ and social
engineering rather than jobs and social mobiltiy. How have they let this happen again?”.
I think that says it all. It just show s, actually, how the Labour Opposition is so
disconnected. It is so out of  touch. It is not listening to  hard-working New Zealanders.
This side of the House knows that John Key’s team is leading in the issues and getting
results in the areas that matter to New Zealanders: having safer communities, having
higher levels of education, having more of our youngsters in education in the first place,
having more jobs, and having an economy that is growing.
This week the National Government actuall y reported on its Better Public Services
targets. Not only do we talk about things; we deliver results. We de liver results in the
areas that matter to hard-working New Z ealanders. So last week, up and down New
Zealand, Labour supporters were picking up th eir jaws off the floor when, instead,
Labour was talking about man bans. It was quite interesting because, to quote one of the
other commentators, Kerre McIvor said in the Herald on Sunday that policies count,
ovaries do not. So, clearly, the Labour Part y cannot find any polic ies, it cannot find
anything that resonates with New Zealande rs, so it is going around counting ovaries.
Well, I do not think that matters to hard-working Kiwis.
On this side of the House—and I am proud to be a female member of the National
